meta.description: Credited to Rosa Parks by every quote site — but Wikiquote files it as unsourced and no book, speech or interview has ever been named.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Have you ever been hurt and the place tries to heal a bit, and you just pull the scar off of it over and over again'?
meta.ogDescription: No primary source pins this line to Rosa Parks. Wikiquote lists it among unsourced quotations and her papers do not contain it.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.sourceLine: This is one of the most-shared sentences attributed to Rosa Parks, and there is nothing behind it. It is not in Wikiquote’s sourced list, where every other Parks quotation names a book, speech or interview; it sits instead on the talk page under “Unsourced.” A full-text search of her papers at the Library of Congress returns nothing, and Quote Investigator has never written it up. That does not make it a fake — it makes it undocumented, which is a different and more honest thing to say.
answer.confidenceText: Credited to Parks everywhere, sourced nowhere: no publication carrying this wording has ever been named.

source.excerpt: Have you ever been hurt and the place tries to heal a bit, and you just pull the scar off of it over and over again.
trail: Wikiquote does not treat this as a sourced Parks quote. It appears on the article’s talk page ↗ in a list headed simply “Unsourced” — the holding pen for lines editors could not tie to any publication.

It is missing from the list where it would belong. The Rosa Parks page ↗ carries about a dozen quotations that each name a source — her autobiography, a 1992 NPR interview, a 1995 speech in Washington. This line is not among them.

The Library of Congress holds her papers, and they do not contain it. A full-text search of the Rosa Parks Papers ↗ for “pull the scar off” returns nothing. That is a signal, not a verdict: the digitised collection is a portion of the whole and handwriting OCR is imperfect. The control phrase “tired of giving in” does return a hit, so the search reaches document text.

Her own book is the obvious place to look, and we could not look inside it. The Internet Archive’s copy of Rosa Parks: My Story ↗ is lending-restricted, so its text could not be searched from here. We are not claiming the line is absent from it — only that nobody who quotes the line cites it.
source.excerptNote: There is no fuller passage to quote. The sentence travels alone, without a surrounding paragraph, in every source that carries it.

source.rightsNote: The work in which this wording first appeared has not been identified, so no rights status can honestly be asserted — and nothing here is public domain. Parks died in 2005; her books, speeches and recorded interviews are modern works still in copyright, controlled by her estate and publishers. If these words are hers, they belong to whichever of those they came from.

author.name: Rosa Parks
author.kicker: The woman who would not move
author.heading: About Rosa Parks
author.metaLine: 1913–2005 · American civil rights activist · Montgomery, Alabama
author.bio: Rosa Louise McCauley Parks was a seamstress and long-serving NAACP secretary in Montgomery, Alabama, whose refusal to give up her bus seat on 1 December 1955 set off the Montgomery bus boycott. Congress later called her the Mother of the Modern-Day Civil Rights Movement, a title that has had the odd side effect of attracting inspirational sentences she never demonstrably wrote. She published an autobiography, Rosa Parks: My Story, with James Haskins in 1992, and her papers are held at the Library of Congress.

context.heading: Why this one is worth checking
lead: The sentence is a good deal more literary than the way Rosa Parks usually talked. Her documented register is flat, exact and unsentimental — “the only tired I was, was tired of giving in” — while this line reaches for an extended metaphor about a wound reopened. That is an observation about style, not evidence, and it cuts both ways: people do not speak in one register their whole lives.

What makes it worth flagging is the shape of its paper trail. A genuine Parks line usually arrives with a book and a page number attached. This one arrives with nothing, and has for as long as anyone has been indexing it.
context.pull: Undocumented is not the same as fake — and it is not the same as verified either.

sourcesVerified.claim: The talk page of the English Wikiquote article "Rosa Parks" lists, under the heading "Unsourced", the sentence "Have you ever been hurt and the place tries to heal a bit, and you just pull the scar off of it over and over again."

A full-text search of the Library of Congress Rosa Parks Papers collection for the exact phrase "pull the scar off" returns zero results. The control phrase "tired of giving in" returns one result against the same collection, and a nonsense control returns zero, so the search does reach document text.

The English Wikiquote article "Rosa Parks" lists roughly a dozen quotations that each carry a named source (Rosa Parks: My Story p. 116; an NPR interview of 1992; a 1995 Washington speech; Theoharis's The Rebellious Life of Mrs. Rosa Parks).
The talk page of the English Wikiquote article "Rosa Parks" carries a section headed "Unsourced" listing quotations attributed to Parks that editors could not tie to a publication.

Wikiquote's sourced section gives "People always said that I didn't give up my seat because I was tired, but that isn't true... the only tired I was, was tired of giving in," citing Rosa Parks: My Story, p. 116, Rosa Parks and James Haskins (1992).

The Internet Archive holds a scan of "Rosa Parks: My Story" catalogued to Parks (1913-2005) and published by Puffin Books, dated 1999 in the item metadata; the full text is lending-restricted and could not be read or searched.

Wikipedia records Rosa Louise McCauley Parks as an American civil rights activist, 1913-2005, best known for her 1955 refusal to move from her bus seat in Montgomery, Alabama, which sparked the Montgomery bus boycott.
